questions.text: Why is the multiplier alone insufficient to identify a constant-division idiom?

options.A: The multiplier identifies only the compiler version, never arithmetic.
options.B: Every odd multiplier implements division by the same constant.
options.C: The divisor also depends on the shift, signedness, and correction sequence.
options.D: The original divisor must always be stored beside the multiplier in rodata.

questions.explanation: For example, 0x66666667 with shift 34 implements signed division by 10, while shift 33 implements division by 5. Width, signedness, and fix-ups are also part of the idiom.

questions.text: A vector loop uses two accumulators with four 32-bit lanes each, then a scalar remainder loop. How should you interpret the two loop bodies?

options.A: Two separate source loops, each processing four elements in total.
options.B: One source loop processing eight elements per vector iteration, then leftovers.
options.C: One source loop processing two elements per iteration, with four-byte padding.
options.D: Two unrelated loops, because vector and scalar instructions cannot share a sum.

questions.explanation: Four lanes times two accumulators gives eight elements per vector iteration. Reduction combines the vector partial sums, and the scalar loop handles the remaining elements.

questions.text: For unsigned division by 7, the idiom computes t = (n * 0x24924925) >> 32, then q = (((n - t) >> 1) + t) >> 2. If n=100 and t=14, what is q?
questions.explanation: 100-14=86; shifting right once gives 43; adding 14 gives 57; shifting right twice gives 14.
